intro.uz: Bu hikoya fermerlar mahsulotini shaharga yetkazib beradigan kichik startap haqida. Oʻqishdan oldin oʻylab koʻring: yangi biznes boshlaganda qanday qiyinchiliklar boʻlishi mumkin?

paragraphs.en: Three years ago, Malika and her friend Bekzod were both working in offices in Tashkent. Malika's parents grew fruit and vegetables in a village in the Fergana Valley, and every summer she heard the same complaint: traders paid farmers very low prices, while people in the city paid a lot for the same tomatoes. Malika wondered if there was a way to connect farmers directly with customers.

The idea was simple. Customers would order a box of fresh seasonal fruit and vegetables online, and the box would be delivered to their door within a day of being picked. Bekzod, who had studied programming, built a basic website in his free time. They borrowed a small van from Malika's uncle and started with twelve customers, most of whom were their own friends and colleagues.

The first months were exciting but exhausting. They both kept their office jobs, so they packed boxes late at night and delivered them at weekends. Then, in their first summer, the van broke down on a hot day, and a whole load of strawberries was ruined before it reached the city. They lost money and several customers. Bekzod admits that he nearly gave up. "If Malika hadn't been so stubborn, I would have stopped," he says.

Instead of giving up, they learned from their mistakes. They invested in a second-hand refrigerated van, and they started to plan their routes more carefully so that the fruit spent less time on the road. They also began to send customers a short message with the name of the farmer who had grown their vegetables. Customers loved this personal touch, and many of them told their friends.

Today, the business works with around forty farming families and delivers several hundred boxes a week. Malika and Bekzod have left their office jobs and employ eight people. Farmers receive better prices than they did from traders, and customers know exactly where their food comes from.

Their advice to young people who want to start a business is practical: start small, listen to your customers, and do not be afraid of failure. "Every problem taught us something," says Malika. "The broken van was the best lesson we ever had."
